blocks.text: The call to “examine yourselves” is addressed to the community as a whole. In a dispute where Paul’s authority is being tested, the demand for proof is turned back toward the Corinthians’ own life in the faith. It is not an invitation to obsessive self-scrutiny, coerced confession, surveillance, or stigma.

Paul’s language about Christ’s power and his own weakness belongs to his defense of ministry. The passage locates Christ’s power amid Paul’s limitations and afflictions, rather than treating those limitations as denied or automatically removed.

Paul invokes witnesses before a planned visit and warns of discipline, but this language does not provide a complete procedure for resolving harm. A fair process requires notice, impartial fact-finding, appropriate corroboration, protection against intimidation, meaningful participation, and review; the witness formula should not be used as a substitute for these safeguards.

The chapter joins claims of power and authority with Paul’s fear that the community may do wrong, his appeal to witnesses, and his statement that authority is for building up. Claims of signs, status, or founding authority therefore do not set ethical review, corroboration, consent, finances, doctrine, law, or safety aside.

Paul’s stated goal of restoration and building up gives an important lens for reading his threatened discipline. It cannot authorize authoritarian control, public shaming, violence, retaliation against critics, or a demand for unity that suppresses truth, dissent, survivor testimony, or necessary conflict. Likewise, the appeal to two or three witnesses belongs to the planned encounter and cannot replace trauma-informed investigation, due process, reporting duties, or appropriate evidence standards in abuse cases.

Paul prays that the Corinthians will do what is right even if that leaves him appearing unapproved. This places the community’s responsible action above a leader’s image or vindication. The closing calls to restoration, encouragement, shared purpose, peace, greeting, and blessing belong to communal repair; they do not settle allegations, validate an office, force reconciliation, or require contact.

The sharp defense of weakness and authority in the preceding chapters belongs to an unresolved conflict. Paul presents hardship and weakness against rival standards, but the opposing side is known only through his polemic; its number, origin, theology, and relation to Corinthian members cannot be securely reconstructed. His testimony should therefore not be turned into founder immunity, suffering competition, charisma capture, or retaliatory discipline.

The larger letter is preserved in early manuscript witnesses: P46 contains most of 2 Corinthians, P99 preserves portions, and major codices provide further witnesses with distinct textual profiles. This concerns the transmission of the letter as a whole, not a direct detail of chapter 13 alone.

sections.title: The Wider Conflict and the Letter’s Transmission
